lessons.title: Botanical Classification and Plant Structure
lessons.body: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) belongs to the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae. Unlike Irish potato, it is a root, not a tuber. The plant has two main types of roots: fibrous roots that absorb water and nutrients, and storage roots that swell to become the sweet potatoes you harvest. The leaves are heart-shaped or lobed, growing on vines that can spread 2â4 meters. Vines are green or purple, depending on variety. At each node (where leaf meets stem), roots can form if the vine touches moist soil. This is why farmers use vine cuttings for planting. The flowers are trumpet-shaped, white or purple, but in Africa many varieties rarely flower; seed is not used for planting. The storage roots develop from adventitious roots that thicken when conditions are right. Understanding this structure helps you: (1) plant vine cuttings at least 3 nodes deep so roots and shoots develop; (2) avoid damaging shallow roots during weeding; (3) recognize that leaf yellowing may indicate root problems. In Africa, common varieties include 'Tanzania', 'SPK004', and 'Ejumula', each with different root shapes and colors. A healthy plant has a balance: too many leaves and few roots means too much nitrogen; too few leaves means poor photosynthesis. By knowing the parts, you can diagnose problems early and take action, such as adding potassium to encourage root swelling.

lessons.title: Growth Stages: From Sprouting to Tuber Formation
lessons.body: Sweet potato growth has four clear stages. Stage 1: Sprouting (0â2 weeks after planting). Vine cuttings develop roots and new shoots. Keep soil moist but not waterlogged. Stage 2: Vegetative growth (2â8 weeks). Vines spread rapidly. Leaves and stems grow. This is when the plant builds its 'factory' for making food. Stage 3: Root initiation and development (4â12 weeks). Storage roots begin to form. They start as thin roots, then swell. This stage is critical: any stress (drought, poor soil, pests) now reduces final yield. Stage 4: Maturity and bulking (12â20 weeks). Roots reach full size. Leaves may start to yellow. In Africa, most varieties mature in 3â5 months, depending on altitude and rainfall. For example, in Nigeria, 'TIS 2532' matures in 4 months; in Uganda, 'NASPOT 1' takes 3â4 months. To manage stages: Water regularly during Stage 3; avoid flooding. Weed early (first 6 weeks) because weeds compete for nutrients. Do not harvest too earlyâroots are still small and starchy. Signs of maturity: skin does not rub off easily, and vines stop growing. You can also dig one plant to check root size. After harvest, cure roots in a shaded, ventilated place for 5â7 days to heal cuts and sweeten the taste. Proper stage management can double your yield from 5 to 10 tons per hectare.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Nutrient Uptake
lessons.body: Photosynthesis is how sweet potato makes food. Leaves capture sunlight, take in carbon dioxide from air, and absorb water from soil. They produce sugars, which are sent to storage roots. More leaf area = more sugar = bigger roots. But too many leaves (from too much nitrogen) can reduce root growth because the plant puts energy into leaves instead. Nutrient uptake: Sweet potato needs 16 essential nutrients. The big three are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). Nitrogen makes leaves green; phosphorus helps root development; potassium is crucial for root swelling and starch formation. A typical recommendation for African soils: apply 200 kg/ha of NPK 15-15-15 at planting, then 100 kg/ha of potassium sulfate (0-0-50) at 6 weeks. But do not guessâtest your soil first. Many African soils are low in phosphorus and potassium. Organic matter (compost, manure) improves soil structure and holds nutrients. Micronutrients like zinc and boron are needed in small amounts; deficiency causes poor root shape. Water is essential: photosynthesis stops if leaves wilt. In dry areas, irrigate every 7â10 days. In humid areas, ensure drainage. Remember: healthy leaves = healthy roots. Remove diseased leaves to stop spread. If leaves turn yellow between veins, it may be magnesium deficiencyâapply Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) at 20 g per plant. By understanding this process, you can time fertilizer applications for maximum root yield.

lessons.title: Environmental Requirements: Temperature, Light, and Humidity
lessons.body: Sweet potato grows best in warm, sunny conditions. Temperature: ideal range is 24â30Â°C. Growth stops below 15Â°C and above 35Â°C. In Africa, lowland areas (0â1000 m) are ideal. Highland areas above 2000 m may have too-cool nights, slowing growth. Frost kills the plant. Light: needs full sun, at least 6â8 hours daily. Shade reduces yield by 50% or more. Do not plant under trees or tall crops. Humidity: prefers moderate humidity (60â80%). High humidity (above 85%) encourages fungal diseases like leaf spot and root rot. Low humidity (below 40%) causes wilting and small roots. In dry savanna areas, plant at the start of rains and mulch to conserve moisture. In humid forest zones, plant on ridges to improve drainage and reduce rot. Rainfall: 500â1000 mm per growing season is ideal. Too much rain (above 1500 mm) can cause waterlogging and root rot. Too little (below 400 mm) requires irrigation. Altitude: from sea level to 2500 m, but best below 1500 m. In East Africa, varieties like 'Kabode' perform well at 1000â1600 m. In West Africa, 'Soliya' is good for lowlands. Always choose a variety suited to your area. You can modify microclimate: use windbreaks to reduce damage, and plant on raised beds if your area floods. Monitor temperature with a simple thermometer; if nights are cold, consider plastic tunnels for seedlings. By matching the crop to your environment, you reduce risk and increase yield.

lessons.title: Soil and Water Needs for Optimal Growth
lessons.body: Sweet potato does best in well-drained, sandy loam or loam soils. Heavy clay soils hold water and cause root deformation. If your soil is clay, add compost, sand, or plant on ridges 30â40 cm high. Ideal soil pH is 5.5â6.5. Acidic soils (pH below 5) need lime; apply 1â2 tons per hectare of agricultural lime before planting. Saline soils are not suitable. Soil depth: at least 30 cm of loose soil for roots to expand. Compacted soil restricts root growth. Water needs: sweet potato is drought-tolerant but yields best with regular moisture. Critical periods: first 2 weeks after planting (root establishment) and weeks 6â12 (root swelling). Water stress during these times reduces yield. In rain-fed areas, plant with the rains. In dry areas, irrigate with 25â30 mm per week. Drip irrigation is efficient; use 2â4 liters per plant per day. Avoid overhead irrigation in humid areas as it spreads disease. Waterlogging for more than 2 days can kill roots. If your field floods, dig drainage channels. Mulching with dry grass or straw reduces evaporation and keeps soil cool. Test your soil every 2 years. Simple test kits are available at agricultural offices. Add organic matter yearly: 5â10 tons per hectare of manure or compost. Rotate sweet potato with cereals like maize or sorghum to reduce pests and improve soil. Never plant sweet potato after sweet potato in the same fieldâthis increases nematodes and diseases. By managing soil and water, you create the best home for your crop.

lessons.title: Common Growth Disorders and Their Causes
lessons.body: Growth disorders reduce yield and quality. Learn to identify them early. 1. Yellowing leaves (chlorosis): often nitrogen deficiency. Apply urea (50 kg/ha) or manure. If yellowing is between veins (interveinal), it's magnesium deficiencyâspray Epsom salt (2% solution). 2. Stunted growth: could be phosphorus deficiency or root damage from nematodes. Add phosphate fertilizer (e.g., DAP) and rotate crops. 3. Root cracking: caused by uneven wateringâdry then wet. Keep soil consistently moist. 4. Root rot: soft, brown, smelly roots. Caused by waterlogging or fungi. Improve drainage, plant on ridges, and treat seeds (vines) with fungicide before planting. 5. Leaf spots and blight: fungal diseases. Remove affected leaves, spray with copper-based fungicide (e.g., copper oxychloride) every 10 days. 6. Vine borers: caterpillars that bore into vines. Handpick and destroy; use neem extract spray. 7. Sweet potato weevil: larvae tunnel into roots. Practice crop rotation, use clean planting material, and harvest promptly. 8. Sunscald: exposed roots turn white and bitter. Mulch to cover roots. 9. Premature flowering: stress (drought, low fertility) causes flowering, reducing root growth. Irrigate and fertilize. 10. Poor root shape: too much nitrogen or compacted soil. Balance fertilizer and loosen soil. In Africa, common disorders also include 'sweet potato virus disease' (SPVD) causing stunting and leaf distortion. Use resistant varieties like 'NASPOT 1' and control whiteflies (aphids) with neem oil. Always keep records: note symptoms, weather, and actions. Share with extension officers. Early action saves your harvest.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sweet Potato Biology for African Agribusiness

This practical reference condenses the biology of sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) into decision-ready guidance for African commercial growers, aggregators, and processors. It focuses on the biological facts that directly affect yield, tuber quality, storage life, and market timing. Use it alongside the earlier lessons in this module as a field and planning companion.

Why Biology Drives Business Decisions

Sweet potato is not a potato. It is a dicotyledonous vine in the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), grown for its enlarged storage roots. This distinction matters commercially: the crop propagates vegetatively from vine cuttings or slips, matures in 90 to 150 days depending on variety and environment, and produces a perishable root that requires careful curing and storage. For African agribusinesses, understanding these biological realities determines planting schedules, harvest windows, post-harvest loss rates, and ultimately gross margins.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, sweet potato is a strategic crop for food security, income generation, and processing into flour, chips, puree, and animal feed. Countries such as Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, Rwanda, Nigeria, Ghana, and Malawi have active value chains. Orange-fleshed varieties (OFSP) carry additional market value because of beta-carotene content, a selling point for nutrition-sensitive buyers and institutional feeding programs.

Botanical Classification and Plant Structure

Sweet potato belongs to the genus Ipomoea, species batatas. It is a herbaceous perennial vine cultivated as an annual. The plant has three commercially important parts:

  • Vines and leaves: The photosynthetic engine. Vines can reach 1 to 5 meters. Leaves are heart-shaped or lobed depending on variety. In some markets, young leaves and tips are sold as a vegetable (e.g., "sweet potato greens" in West Africa).
  • Root system: Fibrous roots absorb water and nutrients. Some fibrous roots thicken into storage roots (tubers) under favorable conditions. Not all roots become tubers, which is why soil and water management directly affect marketable yield.
  • Storage roots: The harvested product. Skin color ranges from white to cream, yellow, orange, red, and purple. Flesh color varies similarly. Shape, size, and dry matter content are variety-specific and influence processing suitability.

For processors, dry matter content is a key biological trait. High dry matter varieties (28 to 35 percent) are preferred for flour and chips; low dry matter varieties are better for puree and fresh consumption. Buyers should specify dry matter requirements in contracts.

Growth Stages: From Sprouting to Tuber Formation

Sweet potato growth follows four overlapping stages:

  1. Sprouting and establishment (0 to 20 days): Cuttings or slips develop roots and new leaves. Moisture is critical. This stage determines plant stand and uniformity.
  2. Vegetative growth (20 to 60 days): Vines expand rapidly, covering the ground. Competition with weeds is highest here. Nitrogen demand peaks.
  3. Tuber initiation and bulking (60 to 110 days): Storage roots form and enlarge. Potassium demand peaks. Water stress now reduces yield and grade.
  4. Maturation (110 to 150 days): Leaves yellow, vines slow, and skins set. Harvest timing affects storage life and sugar content.

Business implication: staggered planting every two to three weeks can smooth labor, cash flow, and market supply. However, staggered planting must match local rainfall and irrigation capacity.

Photosynthesis and Nutrient Uptake

Sweet potato is a C3 plant with high photosynthetic efficiency under warm, sunny conditions. It converts sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into sugars that are translocated to storage roots. Anything that reduces leaf area, such as pest damage, drought, or excessive vine harvesting, reduces tuber yield.

Nutrient uptake is moderate compared with cereals, but sweet potato is sensitive to deficiencies:

Table 1: Approximate nutrient removal by sweet potato per hectare (fresh tuber yield basis)
Nutrient Removal (kg/ha) for 15 t/ha yield Business note
Nitrogen (N) 40 to 60 Excess N favors vines over tubers; split applications.
Phosphorus (PâOâ) 20 to 30 Important for root development; apply at planting.
Potassium (KâO) 80 to 120 Critical for tuber bulking and dry matter; highest ROI nutrient.
Calcium and Magnesium 15 to 25 combined Deficiency reduces storage quality and shelf life.

Source: Adapted from FAO, Crop Information: Sweet Potato, and CIP agronomic guidelines.

Environmental Requirements: Temperature, Light, and Humidity

Sweet potato is a warm-season crop. Optimal growth occurs between 21Â°C and 29Â°C. Temperatures below 15Â°C slow growth; frost kills vines. Tuber formation is best when soil temperature is 20Â°C to 25Â°C. In highland areas of Kenya, Rwanda, and Ethiopia, altitude and cooler nights can extend the growing cycle and reduce dry matter if varieties are not adapted.

Light: full sun is required. Shading above 30 percent reduces yield. Intercropping with tall crops such as maize or banana should be managed to avoid excessive shade.

Humidity: moderate relative humidity (60 to 80 percent) supports growth, but prolonged leaf wetness increases foliar disease risk. In humid coastal West Africa, variety selection for disease tolerance is essential.

Soil and Water Needs for Optimal Growth

Sweet potato performs best on well-drained sandy loam or loam soils with pH 5.5 to 6.5. Heavy clay soils increase root deformation and harvest losses. Compacted soils reduce tuber size and grade. Raised beds or ridges improve drainage and root shape, especially in high-rainfall areas.

Water requirements are approximately 500 to 700 mm per season. Drought during tuber bulking is the most damaging. Irrigation, where available, should maintain soil moisture at 60 to 70 percent of field capacity. Over-irrigation causes vine growth at the expense of tubers and increases rotting.

Table 2: Soil and water parameters for commercial sweet potato production in African conditions
Parameter Optimal range Risk if outside range
Soil pH 5.5 to 6.5 Nutrient lock-up; poor tuber set
Soil texture Sandy loam to loam Deformed roots in clay; low water holding in sand
Seasonal water 500 to 700 mm Yield loss above 30 percent if deficit exceeds 100 mm
Soil temperature 20Â°C to 25Â°C Slow bulking below 18Â°C; heat stress above 30Â°C
Drainage Free draining Waterlogging causes rot and harvest loss

Source: Adapted from FAO crop information and International Potato Center (CIP) sweet potato agronomy resources.

Common Growth Disorders and Their Causes

Disorders reduce marketable yield and processing quality. Key issues for African growers include:

  • Root cracking: Caused by irregular water supply, especially after dry spells followed by heavy rain. Manage with consistent irrigation and mulching.
  • Root deformation (bent, lumpy roots): Caused by compacted or stony soils, or by heavy clay. Use raised beds and deep tillage.
  • Excessive vine growth with few tubers: Caused by excess nitrogen, over-irrigation, or low light. Balance fertilizer and avoid late N applications.
  • Small tuber size: Caused by low potassium, drought during bulking, or high plant density.
  • Skinning and bruising at harvest: Caused by harvesting too early or too late, or by rough handling. Cure roots properly.
  • Viral disease symptoms (mosaic, leaf distortion): Spread by whiteflies and aphids. Use certified virus-free planting material.
SAFETY WARNING: Do not consume or sell sweet potato roots that are severely damaged, rotten, or showing mould growth. Mycotoxins and bacterial soft rots can cause illness. Never use untreated wastewater for irrigation. When handling planting material or harvested roots, use clean tools and wash hands to reduce disease spread. Store cured roots in cool, dry, ventilated conditions away from pesticides and fuel.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Select varieties matched to your market: OFSP for nutrition buyers, high dry matter for processors, local preference for fresh markets.
  • Use certified disease-free vines or slips; never plant material from an unknown source.
  • Plant on raised beds or ridges in high-rainfall areas to protect root shape and drainage.
  • Apply potassium at tuber initiation; avoid excess nitrogen after 45 days.
  • Maintain soil moisture during bulking; drought at this stage cuts yield and grade.
  • Harvest at physiological maturity (90 to 150 days depending on variety) to protect skin and storage life.
  • Cure roots for 4 to 7 days in warm, humid, ventilated conditions before storage or transport.
  • Keep records of variety, planting date, inputs, and yield to improve margins season by season.

Further Reading

  • FAO Crop Information: Sweet Potato â agronomy, soil, and water requirements.
  • International Potato Center (CIP) â Sweetpotato Program â varieties, seed systems, and value chain resources.
  • IITA Sweet Potato Research â African-focused breeding, agronomy, and post-harvest guidance.
  • CGIAR CGSpace Repository â search "sweet potato" for free technical reports and manuals.
  • CABI â crop protection and invasive species information for sweet potato pests and diseases.

Business takeaway: Sweet potato biology is not academic. Every biological fact in this reference maps to a cost, a yield factor, or a market opportunity. Growers who align variety choice, planting date, soil preparation, water management, and harvest timing with these biological requirements will consistently achieve higher marketable yields and stronger margins than those who treat sweet potato as a low-input subsistence crop.

quiz.q: What family does sweet potato belong to?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is in the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae.

quiz.q: Which part of the sweet potato plant stores food?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato forms storage roots, not tubers like Irish potato.

quiz.q: Why are vine cuttings planted at least 3 nodes deep?
options: B) To encourage root and shoot development
quiz.explanation: Nodes are where roots and shoots form, so deeper planting increases establishment.

quiz.q: What is the first growth stage of sweet potato after planting?
quiz.explanation: Sprouting occurs in the first 0â2 weeks, when roots and shoots emerge.

quiz.q: During which stage is water stress most damaging to yield?
quiz.explanation: Water stress during root initiation (4â12 weeks) reduces the number and size of storage roots.

quiz.q: How long does it take for most African sweet potato varieties to mature?
quiz.explanation: Most varieties mature in 3â5 months, depending on altitude and rainfall.

quiz.q: What is the main product of photosynthesis that is sent to storage roots?
quiz.explanation: Photosynthesis produces sugars, which are translocated to storage roots for starch formation.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most critical for root swelling and starch formation?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is essential for root bulking and starch accumulation.

quiz.q: What does yellowing between leaf veins indicate?
quiz.explanation: Interveinal yellowing is a classic sign of magnesium deficiency.

quiz.q: What is a typical NPK recommendation for sweet potato at planting in Africa?
quiz.explanation: 200 kg/ha of NPK 15-15-15 is a common recommendation, followed by potassium later.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for sweet potato growth?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato grows best between 24Â°C and 30Â°C; growth stops below 15Â°C or above 35Â°C.

quiz.q: How many hours of sunlight does sweet potato need daily?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato requires full sun, at least 6â8 hours daily, for good yield.

quiz.q: What is the ideal rainfall range for sweet potato per growing season?
quiz.explanation: 500â1000 mm is ideal; too much rain causes waterlogging and root rot.

quiz.q: At what altitude does sweet potato grow best?
quiz.explanation: Best growth is below 1500 m, though some varieties tolerate up to 2500 m.

quiz.q: What is a recommended action to reduce humidity-related diseases?
quiz.explanation: Planting on ridges improves drainage and reduces fungal diseases in humid areas.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH for sweet potato?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, pH 5.5â6.5.

quiz.q: What type of soil is best for sweet potato?
quiz.explanation: Well-drained sandy loam or loam allows good root expansion and drainage.

quiz.q: How much lime should be applied if soil pH is below 5?
quiz.explanation: 1â2 tons per hectare of agricultural lime raises pH to the optimal range.

quiz.q: What is the critical period for water in sweet potato?
quiz.explanation: Water stress during establishment (first 2 weeks) and root swelling (weeks 6â12) most reduces yield.

quiz.q: How can you reduce evaporation and keep soil cool?
quiz.explanation: Mulching with dry grass or straw conserves moisture and moderates soil temperature.

quiz.q: Which crop rotation is recommended to reduce sweet potato pests?
options: A) Sweet potato after sweet potato
quiz.explanation: Rotating with cereals like maize or sorghum reduces nematodes and diseases.

quiz.q: What causes root cracking in sweet potato?
quiz.explanation: Alternating dry and wet conditions cause roots to crack.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of root rot?
quiz.explanation: Waterlogging promotes fungal growth and root rot.

quiz.q: How can you control sweet potato weevil?
options: B) Practice crop rotation and use clean planting material
quiz.explanation: Crop rotation, clean vines, and prompt harvest reduce weevil damage.

quiz.q: What does premature flowering indicate?
options: B) Stress from drought or low fertility
quiz.explanation: Stress conditions like drought or poor soil cause early flowering, reducing root yield.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of sweet potato virus disease (SPVD)?
quiz.explanation: SPVD causes stunted growth and distorted leaves, reducing yield.

quiz.q: Which variety is resistant to SPVD?
quiz.explanation: NASPOT 1 is known for resistance to sweet potato virus disease.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of curing sweet potato roots after harvest?
options: B) To heal cuts and sweeten taste
quiz.explanation: Curing in a shaded, ventilated place for 5â7 days heals wounds and improves flavor.

quiz.q: What is a sign that sweet potato roots are mature?
options: C) Skin does not rub off easily
quiz.explanation: When mature, the skin adheres firmly and does not rub off easily.

quiz.q: What is a recommended practice to prevent nematode buildup?
options: A) Plant sweet potato every season
quiz.explanation: Rotating with non-host cereals like maize reduces nematode populations.
